strengths: Novel and well-motivated model combining classical sequential social learning (Bikhchandani/Banerjee-style cascades) with a planner who can pay to control private signal precision, formalized as an MDP.
Nice conceptual contrast between altruistic and biased planner objectives, illustrated with concrete, topical applications (targeted digital ads, persuasive LLMs, political campaigns).

Nontrivial theoretical results, most notably convexity of the altruistic value function despite the complication that agents' actions (and hence belief updates) depend on the belief itself, which breaks standard MLR-based arguments; the authors describe a martingale-based inductive proof strategy.

Clean threshold-structured characterizations of myopic and optimal policies for both planner types, yielding interpretable phases (e.g., cascading, last-ditch effort, precision suppression to lock in favorable belief).

The central message—that even a constrained planner (no informational advantage, truthful/symmetric signals, fully observable actions) can substantially move social welfare in either direction—is a compelling and policy-relevant finding, reinforced by numerical experiments showing double-digit to near-100% welfare swings.
Numerical study additionally yields an interesting 'price of anarchy' style comparison between the myopic (decentralized) and optimal (coordinated) altruistic policies.
weaknesses: Full proofs of the main results (including the convexity theorem, arguably the paper's most technically substantial contribution) are relegated to an external, uncited-in-detail companion document [25] not included in the submission; only proof sketches are given, which limits independent verifiability of the central claims.

The optimal biased policy (Theorem 7) is only partially characterized—two of six regions give bounds rather than exact policies—leaving the central 'manipulation' result incomplete relative to the altruistic case.

Numerical evaluation is fairly limited: results are reported as aggregate percentage changes across a parameter sweep and a single illustrative parameter setting (Fig. 2), without sensitivity analysis, confidence intervals, or exploration of how welfare effects scale with cost function shape, discount factor, or baseline precision.

The model is highly stylized (binary state and action, single central planner, homogeneous cost structure, perfectly Bayes-rational agents), which is reasonable for tractability but somewhat undercuts the paper's claims of direct real-world relevance to ad personalization and LLM persuasion, where signals are rarely binary or symmetric.

The related-work discussion omits the large literature on Bayesian persuasion / information design (e.g., Kamenica-Gentzkow and its many extensions), which is directly relevant to a planner controlling information provided to receivers who then act sequentially; this is a significant gap in positioning the contribution.

The paper explicitly leaves open the question of how to prevent/mitigate the biased planner's manipulation, which is arguably the most policy-relevant question raised by the introduction and abstract, but is entirely deferred to future work.

Presentation is dense with many results stated via existence of unspecified thresholds (dA, tA, t1..t5, etc.) without closed-form characterization or intuition for how these thresholds depend on model primitives (p, C, β), limiting the practical/policy takeaways promised in the abstract.

strengths: The paper poses an interesting and timely conceptual question—how a planner who controls private-signal precision (rather than directly paying agents or fabricating information) can steer sequential social learning—motivated by concrete applications such as targeted digital ads and persuasive LLMs.

The extension of the classical Bikhchandani/Banerjee cascade model to include an MDP-based precision-control planner is a reasonably novel combination not previously studied in this exact form, and is clearly differentiated from related prior work on coordinators/information fusion planners.

The threshold-style characterizations of the myopic and (partially) optimal policies for both altruistic and biased planners provide some structural insight into how a planner's behavior should change with public belief.

The paper is careful to state realistic limitations placed on the planner (equal information, symmetric/non-cherry-picked signals, observability) to strengthen the claim that even a heavily constrained planner can meaningfully move welfare.
weaknesses: Central technical results (Theorem 2's convexity proof, Lemma 3, and much of the biased-planner characterization) are only sketched in the paper, with full proofs deferred to an external, uncited/unavailable technical report [25]; as submitted, the manuscript's core theoretical claims cannot be independently verified, which is a serious soundness and reproducibility concern for a conference paper.

The characterization of the optimal biased policy (Theorem 7) is incomplete—several belief regions only give bounds/ranges rather than exact optimal precisions—so the paper does not fully deliver on its stated contribution of 'characterizing' the biased planner's optimal policy.

The empirical/numerical evaluation is thin: results are based on a small set of simulated parameter settings (mostly a single illustrative instance in Fig. 2, and an aggregated bar chart in Fig. 1 without reporting the parameter grid, variance across settings, or sensitivity analysis over δ, p, and the cost function shape). No real data or LLM/ad experiments are used despite these being the headline motivating applications.

The model is highly stylized (binary state, binary signal, scalar precision control, single sequential decision-maker per step, one planner acting against one agent at a time) and it is unclear how well the qualitative conclusions transfer to realistic multi-agent, multi-topic, competitive advertising/LLM ecosystems; the paper does not discuss or test robustness to relaxations of these assumptions.

The 'equivalent information,' 'symmetric signal,' and 'observable control' restrictions, while making the theoretical setting cleaner, are acknowledged by the authors themselves to be unrealistic for the very real-world actors (ad platforms, LLM providers, campaigns) the paper motivates itself with, which weakens the practical significance/policy relevance claimed in the abstract and applications section.

There is no comparison against any alternative control mechanisms, baselines, or prior planner models (e.g., [17], [20]) in the numerical study, making it hard to assess whether the proposed precision-control framework is a meaningfully better or more realistic lens than existing approaches.

The paper's fit to a top-tier AI conference is questionable: the contribution is primarily an economic-theory/MDP-based social-learning result with light-touch, largely qualitative connections to LLMs and ads, and no LLM experiments, no learning algorithms, and no interaction with actual language models are presented despite prominently advertising the LLM connection.

Presentation is dense and reliant on numerous forward references to omitted proofs and definitions, which combined with the deferred technical report reduces overall clarity and self-containedness of the submission.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated extension of the classical sequential social learning model (Bikhchandani-Hirshleifer-Welch/Banerjee) by introducing a planner who can pay to adjust private signal precision, formulated as an MDP.

Nontrivial theoretical contribution: establishing convexity of the altruistic planner's value function despite the dependence of agents' actions on the belief process (where standard MLRP-based arguments fail), which is used to derive a clean threshold-structured optimal policy.
The biased-planner analysis yields an interesting multi-phase characterization that produces intuitive, policy-relevant insights (e.g., decreasing precision to either escape or entrench a cascade).
Compelling and concrete motivating applications (targeted digital ads, political campaigns, persuasive LLMs) that connect the abstract model to timely, practically important settings.

Numerical experiments (via JuliaPOMDP) illustrate the magnitude of the planner's influence on social welfare and quantify a 'price of anarchy' between decentralized (myopic) and coordinated (optimal) precision choices, complementing the analytical results.
weaknesses: Most proofs are only sketched, with full proofs deferred to an external companion document [25] not included in the submission; this makes several central technical claims (e.g., Theorem 2's convexity result) difficult to verify directly from the paper.

The characterization of the optimal biased policy is incomplete—only bounds are given in some belief regions (e.g., condition (C))—so the paper's own stated goal of 'fully characterizing' planner behavior is only partially achieved for the more interesting (biased) case.

The related-work discussion omits the Bayesian persuasion / information design literature (e.g., Kamenica-Gentzkow and its many extensions), which is arguably the most conceptually related line of work to a planner choosing information structures to influence beliefs/actions; this is a significant positioning gap.

Numerical evaluation is limited to a single linear cost-function family and a fairly narrow set of parameter combinations/figures, without broader sensitivity analysis or comparison against alternative cost specifications.

The model retains strong simplifying assumptions (binary state, i.i.d. conditionally symmetric signals, one planner acting on a strictly sequential single line of agents, no strategic reaction to anticipated future planner behavior beyond Bayesian updating) that are only partially discussed as limitations, leaving open how robust the qualitative findings are to relaxing them.

The applications section (ads, LLMs) is illustrative but not empirically grounded—there is no attempt to calibrate or validate the model against real data from these settings, so the practical significance claimed in the abstract/introduction remains speculative.
As presented (likely a short/workshop-style paper), the depth of exposition and proof detail may be insufficient for a top-tier full-length venue relative to the complexity of the claims being made.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated theoretical framework that integrates a dynamic information-design/control problem for a planner with sequential Bayesian social learning among agents, filling a gap between the information design and social learning literatures.

Provides a genuinely difficult and seemingly novel proof of convexity of the altruistic planner's value function despite the unusual state-dependent action rule, which is highlighted as being of independent interest and underpins subsequent structural results.

Gives a rich, well-organized characterization of optimal (or epsilon-optimal) policies for both altruistic and biased planners, identifying multiple qualitatively distinct regimes (no investment, full investment, decreasing/increasing investment, and even non-existence of an optimum requiring epsilon-optimal policies), which yields interpretable, intuitive economic narratives.

Extends the framework thoughtfully to discuss real-world motivating examples (recommendation systems, political campaigns) and a heterogeneous-preference extension for the altruistic case in the appendix.

Complements the theory with an LLM-based simulation pipeline (planner, agent, and message oracle roles) that operationalizes signal precision as tailored text, and shows that emergent LLM planner behavior broadly mirrors theoretical predictions while identifying specific, well-explained deviations tied to documented human-like cognitive biases (underreaction/overreaction, resistance to cascades).
The appendix is thorough and self-contained, with detailed derivations of belief updates, Markovianity of public belief, and full proofs, aiding reproducibility of the theoretical results.
weaknesses: The empirical validation relies on a single LLM (EXAONE Deep 32B) and one narrow synthetic scenario (car-buying), with no cross-model robustness checks or comparison to human-subject data, limiting confidence that the observed alignment/deviations generalize.

Quantitative claims about LLM-optimal policy alignment (e.g., 'deviation is less than 10% for the majority of belief states') are based on informal visual/histogram comparisons rather than statistical tests or confidence intervals, weakening the empirical rigor.

The model's simplifying assumptions (binary state, binary symmetric signal channel, single scalar precision control, identical information sets for planner and agents, full observability of planner actions) are significant restrictions that, while acknowledged in Remark 2, may limit applicability to real algorithmic mediation settings where cherry-picking, framing, or asymmetric information are common.

The theoretical exposition, while rigorous, is extremely dense and notation-heavy (e.g., the convexity proof spans many pages of decision-tree bookkeeping), which may hinder accessibility and independent verification by readers outside this specific technical niche.

Practical implications for regulation/mitigation of biased planners are left largely as future work, with the paper mostly diagnosing the problem (welfare loss from biased planners) rather than proposing concrete mitigation mechanisms.

Limited exploration of sensitivity to key parameters (e.g., different cost function forms beyond linear, alternative baseline precision values, discount factor extremes) in the empirical section, and the LLM experiments appear to use relatively few trials/seeds, raising questions about statistical robustness of the reported welfare and policy-deviation figures.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated framework that combines classical sequential social learning (Bikhchandani/Banerjee-style herding) with a strategic, cost-constrained information-design planner, filling a real gap between the information-design and social-learning literatures.

The theoretical development is rigorous and non-trivial: the convexity proof of the altruistic value function (Theorem 2) requires a careful martingale/decision-tree argument to handle the belief-dependent action rule, and the resulting multi-regime characterizations of optimal altruistic and biased policies (Theorems 3-5) are detailed and internally consistent, including subtle existence issues (epsilon-optimal policies) for the biased planner.

The framework yields interpretable, intuitive qualitative insights (e.g., 'last-ditch' investment near unfavorable cascades, obfuscation by biased planners, distinct policy regimes) that connect cleanly to real-world phenomena like targeted advertising and political persuasion.
The extension of the altruistic planner's problem to heterogeneous agent preferences (Appendix D) is a nice touch that broadens applicability.

The LLM-based simulation is a creative attempt to test whether the stylized model's predictions have any bearing on more realistic, non-Bayesian agents, and the identified deviations (underreaction/overreaction biases, resistance to cascades) are a genuinely interesting empirical contribution connecting to known human/LLM cognitive biases.
The paper is clearly written at a conceptual level, with good motivating examples (Section A) that make the abstract control problem concrete.
weaknesses: The empirical validation is thin relative to the weight placed on it in the abstract and contributions list: only a single LLM (EXAONE Deep 32B) is used in all three roles (agent, planner, oracle), with a single toy scenario (car purchase), no comparison across model families, no human-subject validation, and no reported statistical significance/variance across multiple runs for the welfare and policy-deviation results in Figure 2.

The operationalization of 'signal precision' via an LLM oracle that is simply instructed to produce a message with a 'desired precision' is not independently verified — there is no calibration check confirming that the oracle-generated messages actually induce the intended level of informativeness in the receiving LLM agent, which undermines the claim that the simulation faithfully instantiates the theoretical qi.

The core theoretical model rests on strong simplifying assumptions (binary state, binary symmetric signals, full history observability, identical information sets for planner and agents, single cost functional form) that, while acknowledged, are not stress-tested; it is unclear how much of the rich characterization is an artifact of this narrow signal structure versus a general phenomenon.

The novelty relative to Bayesian persuasion / dynamic information design is somewhat incremental in spirit (the main new ingredient is sequential herding by peers), and several of the qualitative findings (biased planners obfuscate to avoid overturning favorable cascades, thresholds shrink/grow with cost) are intuitive extensions of known single-shot persuasion results rather than surprising discoveries.

The paper's central empirical claims (e.g., 'LLM planner exhibits emergent strategic behavior... mirrors the trends predicted') are supported mostly by visual/qualitative comparison (Figure 2a-b) rather than rigorous quantitative hypothesis testing, limiting the strength of the 'validation' claim.

No code or data release is mentioned for the LLM experiments, and prompt-based experimental details (e.g., exact simulation protocol, number of trajectories, seeds) are sparse, raising reproducibility concerns.

The proofs, while mathematically careful, are extremely long and notationally dense (e.g., the decision-tree argument for Theorem 2 spans many pages), which may hinder verifiability and readability, and the paper does not provide simpler intuition-building examples to make the results accessible.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated theoretical framework combining sequential social learning with a strategic information-mediating planner, addressing an increasingly important real-world phenomenon (LLM-mediated information environments).

Rigorous theoretical contribution: proves convexity of the altruistic planner's value function (a technically involved result of independent interest, given that agent actions depend on the belief state, breaking standard linearity arguments used in prior work like Nyarko 1994), and uses this to fully characterize optimal threshold-structured policies for both altruistic and biased planners.

The characterization of the biased planner's policy is particularly rich and non-obvious, revealing five distinct regimes (including intentional signal obfuscation and non-existence of an optimal policy requiring epsilon-optimal characterizations), which is a nontrivial and interesting finding.

Strong complementary empirical validation using LLMs as agents, planner, and oracle, which (a) identifies concrete non-Bayesian belief-updating biases in LLM agents, (b) shows the LLM planner's emergent policy structurally mirrors the theoretical optimum despite these biases, and (c) quantifies substantial welfare impacts (40-50% swings) even under strict transparency constraints, which strengthens the real-world relevance of the theory.

Clear positioning relative to related literature (social learning, information design/Bayesian persuasion, LLM economic-agent literature), with well-articulated distinctions (e.g., no two-way communication unlike Wei & Anastasopoulos 2022).

Extensive, careful appendix providing full proofs, thoughtful edge-case handling (e.g., epsilon-optimal policies when suprema are not attained), and reasonably detailed experimental/prompting methodology to support reproducibility.
Good real-world grounding via illustrative examples (restaurant recommendation, political campaign) that make the abstract model intuitive and highlight policy/regulatory relevance.
weaknesses: The LLM simulation is based on a single scenario (car purchase) with one model (EXAONE Deep 32B); results may not generalize across different LLMs, prompt designs, or domains, limiting the robustness of the empirical claims.

The 'hybrid setting' and welfare comparisons rely on relatively small-scale simulations (sequences of agents, limited parameter grid) without reported statistical variance/confidence intervals across random seeds, profiles, or multiple LLM runs, making it hard to assess robustness of the quantitative welfare figures (e.g., the 40-50% welfare decrease).

The model's assumptions (binary state/signal, planner-agent information parity, no cherry-picking/lying, full observability) are quite stylized; while these are explicitly acknowledged as simplifications (Remark 2), the paper could better discuss how sensitive the qualitative results are to relaxing them (e.g., partial observability of planner's actions, continuous states).

The generalization to heterogeneous agent preferences (Appendix D) is only sketched for the altruistic case, and the biased planner extension is left as an open question, somewhat limiting the completeness of the theoretical contribution for more realistic multi-type populations.

The paper does not include a human-subject or human-comparison study to validate whether real human agents exhibit similar deviations from Bayesian updating as observed in LLM agents, so the claim that LLM behavior 'mirrors human cognitive patterns' remains somewhat speculative and relies on citing external literature (Rupprecht et al., 2025) rather than direct evidence within this paper.

Some of the proofs (e.g., Theorem 2 convexity proof) are lengthy and dense; while thorough, the paper could benefit from more intuition/illustration in the main text to make the results more accessible to a broader audience.

The related work section, while adequate, could more explicitly discuss quantitative comparisons or baselines from closest prior work (e.g., Wei & Anastasopoulos 2022) to contextualize the magnitude of the paper's contribution beyond conceptual novelty.
